chapter: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
title: Big Sid Catlett's drumming in Fletcher's rhythm section
summary: Catlett took charge, set Fletcher's tempos, fed soloists and could be heard in four-bar solos without overpowering the band.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I'm sure you could probably think of a lot -- okay, there are just a couple more here. I'm sure you could probably think of a lot of other people, but you've a number of times mentioned Syd Catlett, Big Syd.

Big Syd Catlett. Yes, I had the pleasure of being in the rhythm section with him in Fletcher's band. And this happened in the Grand Terrace days too, the "Christopher Columbus" era, along with Chu Berry and Roy. Big Syd was a great fellow. He was a take-charge type of fellow,

When Fletcher would start off, set the tempo, it was there. And He would be prominent. He would n't overshadow you. He was a tenor player's when you're playing ad lib, and trumpet player's dream, as far as playing music, you know, because he'd fill up -- he'd feed you, you know? He's what should feed you, they call in music, that's a musical term, (inaudible) and if you had a little he'd fill up all the holes like the (inaudible) something...
End of a phrase or -- ... in your arrangement --

Phrase -- he was in there all along, and how, and you could hear him because -- this was one time his size -- he was a big guy, and he drummed like that, not overshadow the band, but I mean when he hit something, or took a little solo, (inaudible), even if it was four bars, you didn't have to strain to hear him. You could hear him, you know? And he was always there. And I played with him for quite a spell. He was in that group that had Israel Crosby, so I was going handed me here, to tell you about a little thing that was just (inaudible).
